title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
gist: A DoD budget request seeks $30.3M over five years for 'Polygraph+/Polygraph Next', run by DCSA, focused on AI/ML scoring algorithms and contactless 'standoff sensing' for employee vetting and insider-threat detection, amid a Hegseth-era leak crackdown. The author and quoted experts argue it repeats a long record of failed tech lie-detection efforts because there is no physiological ground truth for lying, making AI likely to add uncertainty and serve mainly as an intimidation/deterrence prop.

insights.claim: A Department of Defense budget request seeks $30.3 million over five years for a program called Polygraph+ (or Polygraph Next) focused on AI/ML scoring algorithms and 'standoff sensing' that takes physiological readings without attaching devices to the subject.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Small but concrete federal budget line for contactless biometric sensing and AI credibility scoring; watch whether Congress approves it and which vendors win contracts.
insights.locator: The US government wants to spend

insights.claim: Polygraph+ would be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts federal background checks, and is intended for vetting prospective employees and 'insider threat detection'; the budget request has not yet been approved by Congress and the specific technologies are undisclosed.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Funding is not yet secured and the tech stack is undefined, so any vendor opportunity remains speculative pending appropriations.
insights.locator: Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence

insights.claim: The Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has increasingly used polygraph tests to hunt leakers, including testing around 50 Joint Staff officers after press coverage of depleted US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Demand for credibility-assessment tech is being driven by political leak-hunting priorities, which makes the program's durability tied to the current administration.
insights.locator: The move comes at a time of high tension

insights.claim: In 2023 the Defense Innovation Unit selected Presage Technologies (claims to measure heart and breathing rate via standard cameras) and Altec Research (a medical sensor firm moving into non-contact sensing) to build deception-detection prototypes, offering clues to what Polygraph+ might use.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: These two firms are the most visible potential beneficiaries of Polygraph+ spending; track DIU/DCSA contract awards to them.
insights.locator: But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues

insights.claim: Altec Research's DIU prototype tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity as contactless deception signals.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Illustrates the shift from contact polygraph sensors to camera/thermal-based remote biometrics, a technology with broader surveillance applications.

insights.claim: Polygraph technology has barely changed since the 1920s, relying on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat; the 1983 Office of Technology Assessment found very limited evidence for employee screening and the 2003 National Research Council called evidence for its efficacy 'weak at best'.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Decades of official skepticism mean AI-enhanced versions face a high evidentiary bar and legal-admissibility headwinds.
insights.locator: Current lie detection technology has barely changed

insights.claim: Even at the American Polygraph Association's claimed 80-94% accuracy, screening the DOD's 2.8 million employees could falsely accuse tens of thousands of people, per the logic of the 2003 NRC report.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Base-rate/false-positive math makes mass screening costly in workforce disruption and litigation risk, regardless of headline accuracy.
insights.locator: Research suggests humans can spot a lie

insights.claim: Polygraph results are subjective across examiners, disproportionately judge people from minority groups as deceptive, and can be beaten with trained countermeasures such as inflating baseline responses with a pin hidden in a shoe.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Bias and gameability create fairness and legal exposure for any agency or vendor deploying credibility-assessment tools.
insights.quote: “If you know how it works, you can beat it,”

insights.claim: The polygraph's main real effect is deterrence, since subjects often confess before the test begins, but that effect depends on people believing the machine works.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: The value of lie-detection tech is largely psychological, so demand can persist even without scientific validity.
insights.quote: “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,”
insights.locator: “If you know how it works, you can beat it,”

insights.claim: Lie detection targets three underlying signals - physiological stress, cognitive load, and conscious concealment effort - and current polygraphs measure only one, so AI-driven multi-modal scoring that combines them could in theory be more accurate and harder to game.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: The bull case for AI lie detection rests on sensor fusion; any credible vendor pitch should address all three channels.
insights.quote: “The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,”
insights.locator: Three things are happening under the surface

insights.claim: Prior tech lie-detection efforts - thermal cameras, pupil trackers, brain scans, the UK's Silent Talker video-based deception score later folded into the EU-funded iBorderCtrl pilot, and the US AVATAR border kiosk using eye tracking, voice and body movement - failed to deliver reliable results outside the lab and quietly faded away.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: The track record argues for skepticism toward AI deception-detection startups and government programs; expect low odds of scaled deployment.
insights.locator: Various new strategies for lie detection

insights.claim: Combining AI with the polygraph may be 'the worst of both worlds' because machine learning can find new patterns in physiological data but cannot validate them against lying without ground truth, since the correctness of historical polygraph records is itself unknown.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Lack of labeled ground truth is a structural barrier to training valid models, a key diligence point for any AI credibility-assessment product.
insights.quote: “Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,”
insights.locator: Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph

insights.claim: Legal scholars expect AI lie detection, like the polygraph, to function more as a psychological prop to intimidate and force confessions than as a scientific tool, and see Polygraph+ as a response to the administration's concern about leaks and loyalty.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Program is politically driven and could face civil-liberties pushback or reversal with a change in administration; watch congressional scrutiny.
insights.quote: “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”
